name: Energy Consumption Problem
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Thermodynamic Bill for Being This Cold
lesson.summary: Moving heat away from a millikelvin qubit stage is thermodynamically expensive by nature, so the continuous power draw of cooling and control infrastructure, not the computation itself, is where a quantum computer's real energy cost lives.
lesson.body:
There is a persistent intuition that quantum computers, because they can solve certain problems with fewer computational steps, must also be more energy efficient than classical computers. For the computation itself, in principle, that can be true for the specific problems where a quantum algorithm offers a real speedup. But that intuition ignores the substantial, continuous energy cost of the surrounding infrastructure, cooling and control, that a quantum computer needs just to operate at all, and that cost is where the energy consumption problem lives.

The physics here follows directly from basic thermodynamics. Removing a given amount of heat from something at millikelvin temperature and dumping it into a room-temperature environment is far more energy-expensive than removing the same amount of heat from something already near room temperature, because the theoretical minimum energy cost of moving heat scales with the ratio of the hot and cold temperatures involved. Cooling from roughly 300 kelvin, room temperature, down to roughly 0.01 kelvin, a typical qubit stage temperature, involves a ratio of about thirty thousand to one. Real dilution refrigerators, compressors, and pulse-tube coolers operate far below this theoretical thermodynamic ideal, so the actual electrical power drawn by a complete cryogenic system, including compressors and supporting electronics, commonly runs into the tens of kilowatts range continuously, for a facility hosting even a single quantum processor, and that is before counting the room-temperature control racks and instrumentation described in the wiring and control problem.

Scaling this up compounds the issue in two ways at once. First, more qubits generally means more wiring and more control electronics, both of which add heat load that the refrigeration system has to remove, increasing the cooling system's own power draw. Second, if some control electronics move into the cold stages of the fridge to solve the wiring bottleneck, as proposed cryo-CMOS approaches suggest, that electronics itself dissipates heat right at the point in the system where removing heat is most thermodynamically expensive, which can partially undercut the benefit of moving it there in the first place.

None of this means useful quantum computers are doomed to be energy hogs forever, since for problems where a quantum algorithm offers a genuine, large speedup, the total energy spent per problem solved could still favor the quantum approach once fault tolerance is achieved. But it does mean the energy consumption problem is a real, physics-grounded constraint on scaling, not just an operating expense line item, and it feeds directly into the infrastructure cost challenges covered next.

It is also worth being clear about what is and is not included in typical comparisons between quantum and classical energy use. Claims that a quantum computer solved a benchmark problem "faster" or with fewer operations usually describe the computation itself, not the continuous kilowatts of cooling and control infrastructure running in the background the entire time the system is powered on, whether or not it is actively computing. A fair energy comparison has to include that background cost, and for machines that are still far from fault-tolerant and useful at scale, that background cost currently dominates.
